items.title: S&P 500 Crypto on a Saturday: The New 24/7 Contracts Measured Against CME
items.content_html:
This started with the perpetual futures. For most of the last decade a "perp" (a futures contract that never expires, held in line with its underlying by a funding payment) was something you traded on an offshore crypto exchange, on crypto. In 2026 that changed fast, and the S&P 500 came along with it:

  • March: trade[XYZ] listed an S&P 500 perp on Hyperliquid (xyz:SP500) as a builder-deployed HIP-3 market, referencing the licensed S&P 500 index for non-US users.
  • May 29: the CFTC approved Kalshi's bitcoin perpetual, the first perpetual listed on a CFTC-regulated US exchange.
  • September 3: Polymarket launched perps on its international platform, with an S&P 500 contract (now listed as USA500) among the first markets. US users are pointed to Polymarket's separate regulated US venue instead.
  • October 6: Kalshi launched its US 500 perpetual, a stock-index perp that US residents can trade. It references the MerQube US Large Cap Index rather than the S&P 500 itself, which is close enough to track but worth knowing.
  • November 2-3: the CFTC let perpetuals on individual US stocks through as well, and CME has gone to court over how these contracts are being approved.

So within a year the S&P 500 went from something you trade on CME (or through SPY) during US hours to something you can trade around the clock on a DEX, a prediction market and a regulated US exchange, in USDC, at leverage most brokers would never offer. The question I actually wanted answered was simple: are these new contracts any good? Do they track the real market, are they fast, and is the weekend price worth anything?

Once I started wiring them up I found they weren't alone. The offshore exchanges had been quietly listing S&P and SPY perps all year (Gate and MEXC in January, Bitget in February, OKX in March, Deribit in September), and tokenized SPY trades in at least five flavors (Backpack's SPYB, which also trades on Binance; Backed's xStocks SPYx; Ondo's SPYon; Robinhood's own SPY token; Bitget's RSPY) on exchanges and in on-chain pools on Solana, BSC, Ethereum and Robinhood Chain. So the tracker grew to all 34 of them. It subscribes to every one at once, converts every quote to E-mini (ES) points, and logs every price change with both the venue's own timestamp and the time it reached me. I left it running from Thursday evening through Monday morning's cash open: about 90 hours, two US cash sessions, a full weekend, and the Sunday 6pm ET reopen. The reference is the CME E-mini itself, 15,983 prints of it.

The short version: the new perps are the best of the bunch. Polymarket's and trade[XYZ]'s contracts lead the whole market by a second or more, and trade[XYZ] tracks CME to about 3 points. The weekend market is real but it doesn't know anything CME doesn't. The leverage is real too, and higher than you'd guess (up to 200x on one contract). And the "free money" gaps between venues mostly turn out to be the price of crossing them.

Quick reference #

The venues worth knowing about, out of 34. "vs CME" is the median premium after converting to ES points (1 point ≈ 1.3 bps at current levels). Lag is measured against the median of all the other active venues during US cash hours; negative means it moves first. The full per-venue table is in the CSV at the bottom.

Venue Type vs CME (pts) Lag (s) Changes/min, cash Changes/min, weekend
Polymarket Perps (USA500) Index perp (anchored) -2.8 22 5.1
trade[XYZ] / Hyperliquid (SP500) Index perp (anchored) -2.5 33 18
OKX SPY-USDT swap SPY perp +1.0 -1.6 11 2.5
Arcus SPY perp SPY perp -11.8 -1.3 13 2.8
Gate SPY perp SPY perp +1.5 -1.1 18 9.8
Bitget SPY perp SPY perp +1.3 -0.7 2.9 0.8
SPYB on Binance Tokenized SPY -4.6 -0.4 5.1 1.1
Kalshi US 500 perp Regulated perp (anchored) +0.3 4.8 0.0
Bitget RSPY Tokenized SPY -9.9 +1.8 25 0.7
MEXC SPY perp SPY perp +0.8 +5.0 5.6 5.5
MEXC SPX500 (three collaterals) Index perp -0.9 +5.5 to +9.8 5.5-6.1 5.5

"Anchored" means the venue is its own instrument family, so it's converted to ES against CME directly and its premium is zero by construction; what's left to measure is how tightly it tracks (trade[XYZ] ±3.0 pts, Kalshi ±5.1, Polymarket ±7.8).

The pitch, point by point #

Weekend liquidity #

This one is true, with an asterisk the size of the weekend.

CME's E-mini trades Sunday 6pm to Friday 5pm ET. Nearly every venue in this test kept publishing a price through the weekend (the exceptions were two on-chain pools and HTX's SPY perp, which went quiet for long stretches), but publishing a price and trading are different things. Kalshi and the ImpliedOpen aggregator published all weekend and changed price exactly zero times. So the useful measure is price changes per minute:

The busy weekend venues are trade[XYZ] (18 changes a minute, about half its weekday rate), Gate's SPY perp (9.8), the four MEXC contracts (5.5 each, which is suspiciously identical to their weekday rate and suggests they're quoting off an index rather than trades), Polymarket Perps (5.1), Arcus and OKX's swap (2.5-2.8). Most of the tokenized SPY on DEXs barely moves on a weekday, let alone a Saturday.

The asterisk is what that weekend price actually means. CME closed Friday at about 7,560 and reopened Sunday about 36 points higher. Here's what the 24/7 venues did in between:

They didn't sit still: they slid as much as 55 points into early Sunday (UTC), then recovered to roughly Friday's level. But none of them priced the gap. The median venue finished the weekend about 7 points below Friday's close while CME opened 36 above it, and not one of the 34 got within 5 points of the reopen. The liquid perps (trade[XYZ], Polymarket) only started to move in the last minute before CME opened, then jumped the full distance in its first minute. The three venues that did drift up 10+ points were thin quotes that disagreed with their own sister contracts, which makes them noise, not foresight.

So on this weekend, the weekend market was a place to trade S&P exposure, not a place to find out where the S&P was going. One weekend is an example, not a law; a weekend with real news on Saturday could look different, and that's the obvious thing to capture next.

Instant liquidity (no T+1 hold) #

Sell SPY at a US broker and the cash settles T+1 (the US moved from T+2 to T+1 in May 2024), and moving it out takes bank rails on top of that. Close a perp on any of these venues and the PnL is in your USDC balance immediately; withdrawing it on-chain is a matter of minutes. Tokenized SPY on a DEX settles in the same transaction as the trade.

The honest caveat is the last hop. "Instant to USDC" is not "instant to dollars in a bank": getting off a stablecoin still goes through an exchange or ramp, and that's where identity checks and bank settlement come back.

Leverage #

"20x and up" is the number that usually gets quoted, but the real caps vary a lot by contract. These are the maximums each venue publishes in its own contract specs or market page:

Venue Contract Max leverage Where the number comes from
MEXC SPX500_USDT (S&P 500 index) 200x MEXC contract API (maxLeverage)
MEXC SPY_USDT 100x MEXC contract API
Gate SPX500_USDT 100x Gate futures API (leverage_max)
Gate SPY_USDT 75x Gate futures API
trade[XYZ] on Hyperliquid xyz:SP500 50x Hyperliquid meta API (maxLeverage)
Polymarket Perps USA500 50x Polymarket's market page (launch coverage said 20x)
Bitget SPYUSDT, SP500USDT 50x Bitget contract API (maxLever)
OKX SPY-USDT-SWAP 50x OKX instruments API (lever); OKX's own explainer page still says "up to 10x"
OKX US500-USDT-SWAP 20x OKX instruments API
Deribit SPY_USDC-PERPETUAL 20x Deribit instrument API (max_leverage)
Arcus SPY perp up to 50x Arcus's homepage
Kalshi US 500 perp about 15x Kalshi's market page at launch, via Finance Magnates (Kalshi's BTC perp is capped at 6x)

Those are the caps for the smallest positions. Most venues tier them down as size grows; MEXC's SPY contract, for example, steps from 100x to 50x, 25x, 20x and 10x. For comparison, CME's E-mini is already leveraged: maintenance margin has been around $25,000 per contract on roughly $378,000 of notional, so about 15x. Kalshi's US 500 is roughly CME-like; everything offshore goes well past it.

The difference that matters isn't the number, it's how liquidation works. Perps liquidate you automatically and continuously, including at 3am on a Saturday, and that's where the weekend data above stops being academic. The Sunday gap was 36 points, about 0.48% of the index:

Leverage Loss on margin from the 36-pt reopen gap From the 55-pt weekend slide
15x (about CME, or Kalshi) 7% 11%
50x (trade[XYZ], Polymarket, Bitget, OKX) 24% 36%
100x (MEXC SPY, Gate SPX500) 48% 73%
200x (MEXC SPX500) liquidated liquidated

That's before fees, funding, or the maintenance margin that gets you liquidated well before you hit 100%. Leverage on a market that gaps when its reference reopens is a different instrument from leverage on a continuous one.

Faster data than CME (for free) #

True, and the gap is big. The free CME feed I used as a reference (TradingView's CME_MINI:ES1!) is delayed by exactly 600 seconds; the delay is announced in the feed itself. Real-time CME data needs a paid exchange entitlement. Every crypto venue in this test streams real time over a websocket for free, stamped with the exchange's own clock, and the on-chain venues can be read straight from the chain: the Uniswap pool on Robinhood Chain was a live eth_subscribe to its swap events, with the price decoded from the event itself.

Real time doesn't mean equally fast, though. Here's who moves first, measured inside two separate cash sessions to check the ordering holds:

Polymarket Perps and trade[XYZ] lead the pack in both sessions: by about 3 seconds on Friday and 1.3-1.5 seconds in Monday's first hour, followed by OKX's swap, Arcus and Gate's SPY perp. All of them react to a sharp 1.5-point market move within the same second. MEXC trails by 5-10 seconds, consistently, and its exchange timestamps arrive about 1.7 seconds old on top of that. Between the two sessions the leaders stayed leaders and the laggards stayed laggards; the venues in the middle shuffled by up to a second or so.

Transport (the venue's timestamp to my receipt) from a home connection was 170-440 ms for most socket feeds, about 1.8 s for MEXC, and 2.8 s for Kalshi, which I could only poll. Absolute numbers carry about ±100 ms of clock uncertainty (more on that in the methodology), but the ranking is solid.

Arbitrage and more efficient markets #

There's clearly mispricing to look at. Here's how far each venue sits from CME after converting to ES points:

A cluster of SPY perps (MEXC, OKX, Bitget, Gate) sits within 1.5 points of CME, and MEXC's three SPX500 contracts sit about 1 point under. Then there are steady offsets: Arcus about -12, Bitget's RSPY token -10, Deribit -10, SPYB on Binance -5. And the tokens on DEXs look all over the place, with Ondo SPYon on Ethereum and BSC at +64 and xStocks SPYx on Solana DEXs at +47, but most of that is bookkeeping, not mispricing. Both tokens reinvest dividends through an on-chain multiplier (about 1.0095 on SPYon and 1.0075 on SPYx, set in the Solana mints' scaled-amount config), so one token is worth slightly more than one share. Venues that quote the raw token sit roughly 0.75-0.95%, or 55-72 ES points, above venues that quote the scaled amount, which is most of the gap.

On top of that there's the 1-3 second lead from the fast perps, and the weekend, where the whole complex sat 36 points away from where CME was about to open. That's the case for "more efficient markets": these venues add price discovery outside CME hours and outside CME's fee structure. The catch is whether any of it is yours.

What arbitrage actually costs #

Fees #

One ES point is about 1.3 bps. An arb has two legs, and you open and close both, so that's four fills. At an illustrative 5 bps taker fee per fill, a round trip costs about 20 bps, or roughly 15 ES points, which is more than most of the gaps in the chart above. Maker rebates and fee tiers change this a lot, which is exactly why the people doing it at scale are the ones on the lowest tiers. Perps also charge (or pay) funding, which accrues the whole time you hold the position.

This is also why the steady premiums are steady. Arcus sitting 12 points under CME with only ±3.7 points of tracking error isn't a mispricing anyone forgot to trade; a stable offset like that is the market pricing in fees, funding and the cost of moving capital between venues. A gap you can arbitrage is one that moves, not one that sits still.

Slippage #

The quote isn't the fill. Many of these books are thin: several of the DEX rows went a full minute or more without a single price change for over 90% of the capture, and when I investigated one Solana SPYB pool that was disagreeing with the rest, it turned out to trade about $7,000 a day. Its price was simply stale. A gap on a venue like that disappears the moment you try to trade into it, usually against you.

Capital has to be pre-positioned on both sides too. Moving USDC between exchanges takes minutes, which is several lifetimes of a 2-second lead.

Colocation #

The lead/lag numbers make the fast perps look catchable from home: a 2-3 second head start, and I was receiving their updates in a few hundred milliseconds. But the market makers who create that lead are colocated or close to the venues' matching engines, see the same move in single-digit milliseconds, and have usually already traded it by the time a home connection hears about it. You aren't competing for a 3-second window; you're competing for the first few milliseconds of it, against people who paid to be there.

Premium RPC and websocket feeds #

The free tier is not built for this. Two things I hit during the capture:

  • Jupiter rate-limited the three Solana token feeds 733 times, which forced them from a 3-second poll to a 30-second one. On-chain reads through public RPC endpoints get similar treatment.
  • Several exchanges silently drop a websocket that doesn't send the keepalive they expect (MEXC after about a minute, Bitget after about two), and TradingView drops one that answers its heartbeat in the wrong framing. My first version of the tracker reconnected TradingView about three times a minute and the MEXC contracts dozens of times an hour until I fixed it. Each reconnect is a few seconds of blindness, which would be fatal to any strategy that depends on seeing a move first.

Serious operators pay for dedicated RPC nodes, premium data feeds, and the engineering to keep them up. That's a fixed cost you have to earn back before the arb pays anything.

No KYC? #

Two different questions get mixed up under "no KYC": what a venue asks you for, and what actually stops someone it says it doesn't serve. A terms-of-service page that says "not available to US persons" isn't a control. So for each layer, here's what is actually enforced and by what.

kycnot.me, a directory that grades exchanges by how much identity checking they do, gives a useful vocabulary: level 0 is "Guaranteed no KYC" and level 4 is "Mandatory KYC" ("required for key features, and may be required arbitrarily at any time"), with "Rare" and "Shotgun" KYC in between for services that only ask when something gets flagged. It's built around bitcoin and monero, so of the venues here it only lists Binance, at level 4. The rest sort themselves into three layers.

Custodial exchanges: KYC is the control #

Venue What's required
Binance "All new users are required to complete [Verified] to access Binance products and service offerings" (FAQ)
Deribit "Deribit requires clients to perform personal verification (KYC) before they will have access to deposits" (deribit.com)
Kalshi "US-based Kalshi users who have completed KYC verification are eligible to apply" (help)
Bitget "You will need to comply with our identity verification procedures before opening an Account" (terms)
Phemex ID plus a selfie with liveness detection; without it the 24-hour withdrawal limit is 0 USDT (guide)
MEXC unverified users are told to "complete real-name verification before continuing with withdrawals" (KYC FAQ)

These hold your money, so their rules have teeth. A VPN changes your IP address; KYC checks your passport, so an ID or address in a restricted country fails at onboarding wherever your traffic appears to come from, and bank and card deposits carry a country of their own. Phemex and MEXC will take a deposit without ID but won't let it back out. And the enforcement continues after sign-up: MEXC's user agreement says that if "you have given false representations of your location or place of residence," it can act "including termination of any Account immediately and liquidating any open positions." On a custodial exchange the risk isn't getting blocked at the door; it's getting found out later with a leveraged position open and your collateral on their books.

Wallet-only perps: the website is the control #

trade[XYZ], Polymarket's international site and Arcus all start with connecting a wallet. trade[XYZ]'s terms say "To use the Interface, you must connect a non-custodial wallet," and Polymarket's sign-up takes Google, an emailed code or a wallet, with no ID step. The only technical check is an IP block on the website, which a VPN defeats, and underneath the website the chain checks nothing at all: Hyperliquid's order book accepts any signed order from any address. Both trade[XYZ] and Polymarket ban VPNs in writing ("You must not use a VPN, proxy, Tor, or similar to circumvent geo-blocks or our eligibility rules," and Polymarket "strictly prohibits the use of VPNs or similar tools to bypass geographic restrictions"), but on these venues that's a contract term, not a mechanism.

DEX pools: nothing is the control, until the issuer acts #

And you don't need a perp venue at all. The tokenized SPY pools in this test trade straight from a wallet, with no account and no front end required. Jupiter is just an aggregator that routes a swap across Solana pools; the rest are individual pools on Solana, BSC, Ethereum and Robinhood Chain. It's peer-to-pool rather than peer-to-peer: your wallet trades against a smart contract holding both tokens, at a price set by the pool's balance. At the end of the capture they were doing real volume:

Token Chain Pools 24h volume
Robinhood's SPY token Robinhood Chain 30 $13.2M
xStocks SPYx Solana 28 $2.55M
SPYB BSC 9 $691k
Ondo SPYon Ethereum 5 $25k
Backpack's SPYB Solana 5 $25k
Ondo SPYon BSC 1 $156

That's about $16.5 million a day of S&P exposure changing hands with no identity check anywhere in the trade. The issuers' US-person restrictions are enforced where the issuer is actually involved, at minting and redemption (Ondo, for example, runs KYC and AML checks there), not in the pool.

What the issuers do keep is a kill switch, written into the tokens themselves. I read the token contracts directly:

Token What the issuer can do on-chain
SPYx (Solana) freeze any holder's account, pause all transfers, and move or burn tokens from any wallet (a "permanent delegate"); it can also switch on a transfer hook later
Backpack's SPYB (Solana) the same: freeze, pause, permanent delegate, transfer hook available
Ondo SPYon (Solana) freeze and pause, transfer hook available; no permanent delegate
Ondo SPYon (Ethereum, BSC) an upgradeable contract (the issuer can replace its logic), with role-gated mint and burn-from-any-address functions
Robinhood's SPY token an upgradeable contract with a pause switch
SPYB (BSC) an upgradeable contract with role-gated permissions

None of them was paused when I checked, none of the Solana mints freezes new accounts by default, and none has an active transfer hook, so there's no allowlist in force today. Nothing stops anyone buying. The control is after the fact: an issuer that decides a wallet shouldn't hold its token can freeze it, and for SPYx and SPYB, take the tokens back.

Wallet-only also cuts the other way. Arcus lost about $2.23 million to a sub-account bug on November 10, two days before this capture started. Non-custodial means nobody can freeze your account; it also means nobody is standing behind it.

What a VPN actually changes #

On a custodial exchange, nothing that matters: the control is your identity. On a wallet-only perp venue it gets you past the only technical check there is. On a DEX pool there's no check for it to get past. What's left in the last two cases is the terms you agreed to, the issuer's ability to freeze or claw back tokens later, and the money itself: a wallet still needs USDC from somewhere, and the main on-ramps are the KYC'd exchanges above. The no-KYC services kycnot.me tracks (instant swap services, and peer-to-peer markets like Bisq and RoboSats) deal in bitcoin and monero, not S&P exposure, so any route to an index position without KYC ends on-chain.

None of this makes it allowed. Being able to reach a venue and being permitted to use it from where you live are separate questions, and the second one is about the venue's terms and your local law.

How this was measured #

  • Conversion to ES. Each instrument family (SPY products, index perps, Kalshi, Polymarket, trade[XYZ]) gets one multiplicative ratio to ES, learned from the CME tape at the CME print's own timestamp (the free feed is 600 s delayed, so every comparison looks up each venue's quote at the moment the CME trade happened, not the moment I received it). A venue's premium is how far it sits from its family after that.
  • Speed. From a log of every price change (about 1.16 million of them over 3.7 days, half of them from trade[XYZ] alone), not periodic snapshots. Each venue's premium is removed, the "market" is the median of the venues that change price at least twice a minute (leaving the venue being measured out), and lag is the shift, in 250 ms steps, that best lines up each venue's five-second moves with the market's. It's measured separately in the Friday session (6.5 hours) and the first hour of Monday's, then averaged by length. Lags with correlation below 0.2 are dropped.
  • Clock. My PC's clock wandered by more than a second during the capture as Windows slowly corrected it, and I changed networks partway through. Transport times are corrected per tick against a drift curve built from the fastest feeds and pinned to an NTP check, so differences between venues are reliable, but absolute values carry about ±100 ms.
  • Weekend test. Each venue's level is the median of its quotes in the five minutes before CME's Friday close and the five minutes before the Sunday reopen; CME's gap is its first five minutes of prints against its last five before the close. Measuring each venue against its own Friday level makes the test independent of its premium. There's a 9-hour hole in the capture on Sunday (07:38-16:50 UTC); it doesn't touch the close or reopen windows.

Takeaways #

  • For speed: Polymarket Perps and trade[XYZ] lead the market by 1.5-3 seconds, react within the same second, and rarely sit flat.
  • For the level: the SPY perps on OKX, Gate, Bitget and MEXC track CME within 1.5 points; MEXC's SPX500 contracts within 1.
  • For weekends: trade[XYZ] and Gate's SPY perp are the most active, but on this weekend no venue said anything about where CME would reopen.
  • Avoid for timing: MEXC is accurate on level and consistently 5-10 seconds late.
  • On arbitrage: the gaps are real, but most of them are the cost of crossing them. What's left belongs to whoever has the lowest fees, the deepest pre-positioned capital, and the shortest wire.

Full per-venue scorecard (35 rows: every instrument plus the CME reference, with premium, tracking error, lag per session, transport, changes per minute by market state, and weekend move): sp500-24-7-venue-scorecard.csv

Nothing here is financial or legal advice. These are 90 hours of measurements from one home connection, including one weekend; treat them as a snapshot, not a ranking that will hold.

items.title: Fleet Policies as Code (How to add CIS Benchmarks)
items.content_html:
Fleet's Policies page has an "Add policy" button. Click it, and you get a form: name, description, query, resolution, one at a time. If you've got a benchmark with a thousand controls in it (say, the CIS Benchmark for Windows 11), that UI is telling you, pretty clearly, to go click that button a thousand times.

That's not actually true. Fleet policies are defined by a plain YAML spec (apiVersion, kind: policy, spec: {name, query, description, resolution, platform, critical}), and fleetctl apply -f <file> will take a file with as many of those as you want and create or update all of them in one shot. It's genuinely one command for however many hundreds of policies are in the file. The problem isn't that this doesn't exist, it's that there's a real gap between where you'd learn this is possible and where you'd actually go looking.

Where the UI points you, and where the docs point you #

The web UI's "Add policy" flow is single-record only, there's no "import" or "upload YAML" button anywhere in Policies. If you only ever interact with Fleet through the browser, there's no path from that screen to "you can define a thousand of these in a file and apply them at once."

Fleet's own policy-as-code / GitOps documentation does talk about YAML and automation, but at the level of "here's the schema, here's how GitOps drives your Fleet config from a repo." The explanation is abstract and aimed at people already committed to running Fleet via a GitOps pipeline (a whole separate setup: a repo, CI, fleetctl apply wired into a workflow). It reads as infrastructure for managing Fleet declaratively, not as the thing you'd reach for to bulk-load a benchmark on an afternoon. Nothing connects "here's the YAML schema" to "and therefore, here's how you'd dump an existing large policy set in one command outside of a full GitOps setup."

So you end up with the UI implying one-at-a-time is the only way, and the docs implying bulk-apply is only relevant if you've already bought into GitOps, when actually fleetctl apply -f policies.yml just works standalone, logged in with a regular user account, no pipeline required.

What it looks like once you know to look for it #

A policy spec is nothing unusual: a SELECT query, a name, a description, a remediation note.

apiVersion: v1
kind: policy
spec:
  name: CIS - Ensure 'Device Enumeration Policy' is set to 'Block all (most restrictive)'
  platform: windows
  description: 'This policy is intended to provide additional security against external DMA-capable devices...'
  resolution: To establish the recommended configuration via configuration profiles, set the following Settings Catalog path to Block all (most restrictive). Dma Guard\Device Enumeration Policy
  query: SELECT 1 FROM registry WHERE path = 'HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceInstall\Settings\DeviceEnumerationPolicy' AND data = '0';
  tags: framework:CISv8.1, benchmark:win11, level:BL, platform:windows, category:dma-guard, requirement:standard, critical:false, control:device-enumeration-policy-is-block-all, cis_safeguard_ids:CIS28.1
  purpose: Enforcement
---

Stack as many of those as you want in one file, separated by ---, and:

fleetctl config set --address https://your-fleet-instance.example.com
fleetctl login --email you@example.com --password "..."
fleetctl apply -f bl_win11_intune.yaml
[+] applied 34 policies

No GitOps repo, no CI job, no YAML pipeline, just a logged-in fleetctl session and one command. It's idempotent too: apply upserts on policy name, so re-running it after editing the file just updates the existing policies instead of duplicating them. Once applied, they show up in the regular Policies UI exactly like a policy someone clicked "Add" to create: pass/fail evaluated automatically on Fleet's normal schedule against every matching host, no different from any other policy. The bulk-import is invisible after the fact; it's only the path to get there that's missing from the UI.

The one thing worth knowing before you do this #

Policies in Fleet are platform-scoped (and team-scoped), not host-scoped. Applying a platform: windows policy file runs it against every Windows host Fleet manages, not just the one machine you had in mind when you went looking for this. That's the expected behavior for something meant to give you fleet-wide coverage, but it's worth knowing before you dump a thousand new rows into a shared Policies dashboard that other people also look at: plan the scope of what you're applying, not just whether you can.

fleetctl delete -f does not undo this #

If you apply a file and then decide you want it gone, the obvious move is fleetctl delete -f <same file>. Don't bother: for kind: policy specs it's a silent no-op. It runs without printing an error, exits cleanly, and the policies are all still sitting there unchanged. Watching the actual HTTP calls it makes (--debug) confirms why: it only ever hits GET /config and GET /version, never touching the policies endpoint at all. Apparently delete only knows how to handle config/fleet kind specs, not policies, and it fails silently instead of telling you that.

The real way to remove a batch of applied policies is the REST API directly:

curl -X POST "https://your-fleet-instance.example.com/api/v1/fleet/global/policies/delete" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"ids": [1,2,3, ...]}'

Grab the IDs from GET /api/v1/fleet/global/policies first. There's no delete-by-name or delete-by-file option, it's strictly a list of numeric policy IDs, so if you applied the file as a clean slate (nothing else in the Policies list), the IDs are just whatever contiguous range apply created.

items.title: Picking a Browser MCP Server: Twelve Options Compared
items.content_html:
A while back I went through the handful of Camoufox-based MCP servers and wrote up which one to pick. That post kept getting the same follow-up question in one form or another: "okay, but what about the ones that just use my normal Chrome?" Fair. The Camoufox projects solve a specific problem (anti-detection for scraping), but plenty of people just want an agent to drive the browser they're already logged into. So this is the larger list: every browser-control MCP server I've actually looked at, twelve in total, split into three genuinely different families. The Camoufox five are still here, but now sitting next to the Chrome-session servers and the agent-framework wrappers they're usually weighed against.

Two things up front, because they change how you read the rest. First, "tool count" is not quality; it's a philosophy statement about how much the agent is allowed to micromanage the browser. Second, these three families don't compete for the same slot: one of them is a tool an LLM calls step by step, one is an agent that decides its own steps, and one is a stealth-first variant of the first. If you're comparing across families you're probably comparing the wrong things.

Quick reference #

Repo Language Tools Approach Harness
Saik0s/mcp-browser-use Python (FastMCP) small (agent) MCP wrapper around the browser-use agent Own browser via Playwright
browser-use/browser-use Python / TS library The agent framework itself, not an MCP server Own / system Chrome / cloud
BrowserMCP/mcp TypeScript 12 Drives your existing Chrome profile via extension Your Chrome
BrowserTools MCP JavaScript 16 Observability/debugging, not clicking Your Chrome (DevTools open)
hangwin/mcp-chrome TypeScript 26 General assistant on your daily Chrome Your Chrome
Agent360dk/browser-mcp JavaScript 40 Your real Chrome, with a human in the loop Your Chrome
ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp TypeScript 59 Official DevTools team server (Puppeteer) Own Chrome / connect / Android
whit3rabbit/camoufox-mcp TypeScript 17 Bounded, high-level actions to cut round-trips Camoufox
rlgrpe/camoufox-browser-cli Python (FastMCP) 21 CLI reshaped as MCP, persistent daemon Camoufox (Linux/macOS)
redf0x1/camofox-mcp TypeScript 47 Split server/client, remote-friendly Camoufox, remote
Sekinal/camoufox-mcp Python 127 Full Playwright surface, 1:1 Camoufox (Docker)
RobithYusuf/mcp-camoufox JavaScript 99 Scraping/stealth-first Camoufox

That 17-to-127 spread on the Camoufox side, and 12-to-59 on the Chrome side, is the whole story in one row: these aren't twelve implementations of the same idea. They're twelve different bets on how much control an LLM agent actually needs, and, on the Chrome side, how much of your real, logged-in, cookie-laden browser it's allowed to touch.

Full tool-by-tool CSVs are linked at the bottom: a 199-row capability matrix across ten of the twelve, and a 153-row per-project inventory of every registered tool.

Family 1: the agent frameworks #

These are the odd ones out, and I'm listing them first specifically so you stop comparing them tool-count to the rest.

browser-use/browser-use isn't an MCP server at all; it's the agent library underneath a bunch of them (~118k stars, Python + TypeScript). You hand it a goal and a model and it decides the clicks itself. It runs a local Playwright browser, your system Chrome via Browser.from_system_chrome(), or a cloud browser, and you can wire CDP for remote. The strength is raw agent power and model choice: custom actions via @tools.action, structured output, the BU2 model, and a Claude "browser toolset" integration. The catch is the obvious one: you build the integration, you pay for an LLM per run, and managed stealth/cloud costs money.

Saik0s/mcp-browser-use is the MCP wrapper around that (~1k stars, MIT). It exposes run_browser_agent and run_deep_research plus skills CRUD and task/health observability, and because agent tasks run 30–120 seconds it uses an HTTP daemon on :8383 rather than stdio (with mcp-remote for stdio-only clients). It needs an LLM key (twelve provider options) because it is an agent; the LLM picks the steps. There's a genuinely clever bit: the Skills system records a session, extracts the site's underlying "money" API call, and replays it dramatically faster than re-driving the DOM. It's labeled super alpha, and it's heavyweight, but if your problem is "go research this and come back with an answer," none of the tool-per-action servers below will do it.

The reason these two don't appear in the tool matrix below is structural: they don't expose click_element and fill_input as MCP tools for your client to orchestrate. They take a goal. Different category.

Family 2: drive your real Chrome #

This is the group people actually mean when they say "browser MCP." The pitch is identical across all of them: attach to the Chrome you're already signed into, so logins, cookies, extensions, and your fingerprint all carry over, and you avoid re-authenticating or tripping bot checks. They differ in how they attach, how much they expose, and how much rope they give the model.

BrowserMCP/mcp (BrowserMCP.io, Apache-2.0, ~7.2k stars, 12 tools) is the one that started the "use your existing profile" idea, adapted from Microsoft's Playwright MCP to target your live browser instead of a fresh instance. It works, but I'd be careful recommending it for new work: the repo is only a handful of commits, can't be built standalone (it depends on a private monorepo), and appears to have gone quiet since around April 2025. Historically important, practically superseded.

AgentDeskAI/browser-tools-mcp (BrowserTools MCP, MIT, ~7.3k stars, 16 tools) is the odd one out in this family because it mostly doesn't click things. It's an observability tool: it streams console logs and errors, network logs and errors, storage, the selected element, and page info, and runs Lighthouse audits (accessibility, performance/Core Web Vitals, SEO, best practices) against the page you're looking at. You open DevTools (F12) and it reads what's happening. The v2 rewrite tightened security a lot (loopback-only, per-run auth token, credentials scrubbed, cookies opt-in), which matters because v1.x had a critical vulnerability, so upgrade if you're on it. If your job is "tell me why this page is broken," this is the right family member. If your job is "click through this flow," it's the wrong tool entirely.

hangwin/mcp-chrome (MIT, ~12.5k stars, 26 tools) is the feature-rich generalist. It's a Chrome extension-based server (Streamable HTTP on :12306, or stdio) that drives your daily Chrome with no separate browser process. The tool surface is broad: windows and tabs, navigation, element and full-page screenshots, network capture and a debugger, raw HTTP requests, content and interactive-element extraction, console, click/fill/keyboard, bookmarks, history, plus a semantic search across your open tabs backed by a local vector DB. There's even a visual editor for Claude Code and Codex. It's the direct competitor to Agent360 below: more features, less safety.

Agent360dk/browser-mcp (MIT, ~53 stars, 40 tools) is newer and smaller but takes the most interesting angle: human-in-the-loop. Its browser_ask_user overlays a prompt on your screen for 2FA, CAPTCHA, or credentials, then continues the same signed-in session, which is exactly how you handle a site with no API and a login you can't automate cleanly. It also does CAPTCHA solving (reCAPTCHA v2/v3, hCaptcha, Turnstile), CORS bypass via browser_fetch, provider token-extraction guides (Stripe, HubSpot, Slack), combobox and date handling, iframe support, file upload, and network waiting, with up to 20 concurrent agents each in a color-coded tab group. It's also honest about limits (background-tab input, :hover, untrusted events) instead of pretending everything succeeds. Caveats: Windows wasn't verified at the time of writing, and the local bridge is unauthenticated on loopback.

I actually verified Windows since, and the thing worth flagging isn't in the tool count: nothing stops you from driving Agent360 with a plain client SDK instead of an agent, at which point there's no LLM call per run at all, you script the browser the same way you'd script against an API, just with hand-written field-fill logic instead of a model deciding each step. I used it this way to drive a real, already-logged-in Brave profile through a multi-step form end to end (dropdowns, a date picker, a handful of field types), with zero model calls and the real session's cookies intact. That's what makes it a genuine alternative to Camoufox on a non-headless desktop you don't want to hand a separate automation profile to, you keep your real login, and you're not paying for or waiting on an LLM for deterministic steps you can just write down. One real gotcha from doing this: tool calls (including the initial handshake) can hang indefinitely with no error at all, so put a timeout and retry-on-a-fresh-session around every call yourself.

ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp (Apache-2.0, ~53k stars, 59 tools) is the official Chrome DevTools team server, and it's the one I'd trust with CI. It's Puppeteer-based and launches its own Chrome by default (Chrome 136+ blocks remote debugging on your default profile anyway), though it can connect to a running instance or an Android device. It has the deepest debugging surface here: performance traces with CrUX insights, network analysis, screenshots, console with source-mapped stack traces, and reliable auto-waiting automation. --slim and --headless modes keep it light for basic tasks. Because it's Google-maintained and stable it's the recommended base for building a browser subagent, the trade-off being it's the weakest at "reuse my logged-in session," which is the entire reason the other four exist. Note the privacy default: it sends usage stats and optional CrUX data unless you pass --no-usage-statistics and --no-performance-crux.

That "weakest at reusing my logged-in session" line isn't theoretical, I went looking for a way around it before settling on Agent360, and every path dead-ended the same way. --remote-debugging-port relaunch means killing and relaunching your whole multi-profile browser, not just opening a debug socket next to it. Chrome 144's chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging "automatic connection" promises exactly this but hits an undocumented 404 in practice. And --autoConnect itself, per the CLI's own docs, only targets Chrome's own default-profile path by channel name (stable/beta/canary/dev), it has no concept of Brave, or of a second Chrome profile, so it doesn't generalize to "attach to the specific already-logged-in browser instance I'm looking at" at all. Copying the live profile's cookies into a fresh automation profile technically works, but duplicating session state into a second location just to satisfy a debugging protocol is the kind of workaround that creates its own security question. If your whole requirement is "drive the real desktop browser I'm already signed into, non-headless, without spinning up or cloning a profile," chrome-devtools-mcp is not that tool no matter how good its debugging surface is, that's the gap Agent360's extension-bridge approach actually closes.

Family 3: the stealthy Camoufox ones #

If Family 2 is about driving a browser you already trust, this family is about a browser that doesn't want to be recognized. Camoufox is a Firefox fork with anti-detection patched in at the C++ level rather than bolted on with JavaScript overrides, and there are five MCP wrappers around it. These keep their own section because they're solving a different problem: not "reuse my session," but "look like a normal human on a site that hates automation."

whit3rabbit goes bounded and high-level (17 tools). browse does nav-and-scrape in a single call, and browse_sequence takes an array of typed actions (click, hover, fill, type, select, press, waitFor, scroll, evaluate) that all execute in one browser-side pass, so you're not paying a round-trip per step. Fewest tools of the five, and for most scraping that's a feature.

Sekinal goes granular and mirrors Playwright almost 1:1 (127 tools): emulation (emulate_device, emulate_network, set_geolocation, set_timezone, set_locale, set_color_scheme), performance debugging (get_performance_metrics, get_navigation_timing, get_resource_timing, get_memory_info, get_long_tasks), and pixel-level pointer control (mouse_drag_xy, mouse_wheel, mouse_down, mouse_up). It also ships a VNC bridge on :6080 so you can watch the agent drive the browser live, genuinely useful when something misbehaves and you don't want to guess blind. Ships as Docker, which sidesteps host-OS problems entirely.

RobithYusuf goes pragmatic and stealth-first (99 tools): click_turnstile uses Bezier-curve mouse paths specifically to beat Cloudflare Turnstile checkboxes, alongside detect_anti_bot, mouse_drift, and record/replay for humanized paths. On the data side there's scrape_page, extract_structured, and extract_table, plus session portability via cookie_export/cookie_import and storage_state_save/storage_state_load.

The other two are narrower bets. rlgrpe is CLI args reshaped into MCP tools against a persistent background daemon (browser_install/browser_close). Light, but Linux/macOS only, so it's out on Windows. redf0x1 splits into a server/client model meant for remote deployment, where the browser runtime lives somewhere other than the agent, the right call if you're driving this from a lightweight VPS or serverless function.

What the tool matrix actually shows #

I mapped ten of these twelve against each other capability-by-capability (the two agent frameworks are excluded because their tool surface is a goal, not a command list), and the split is cleaner than I expected. It's in the comparison CSV (199 rows) if you want to cross-reference, but the shape of it:

  • Assertions and verification are almost Camoufox-only. verify_value, verify_text_visible, verify_element_hidden, assert_url_matches, assert_text_present. The Chrome-session servers mostly don't expose self-checking tools. If your workflow needs the agent to confirm a state rather than assume it, that's a real gap on the Chrome side.
  • Humanization lives on the Camoufox side. humanize_type, humanize_click, mouse_drift, record/replay mouse paths, click_turnstile. The Chrome-session servers drive your real browser and lean on the fact that your real browser already looks human; they don't synthesize human motion, because they don't need to.
  • Debugger and CDP depth is Chrome-side. Heap snapshots and memory summaries, CSS-computed styles for the selected element, network request detail, performance traces and CrUX, emulation presets, and Lighthouse audits are things the Camoufox wrappers largely don't do. chrome-devtools-mcp alone owns most of this.
  • Human-in-the-loop is Chrome-side only. browser_ask_user and browser_provide_feedback have no Camoufox equivalent, which makes sense, since a headless stealth context has no human watching it.
  • Batch/sequence execution is Camoufox-side. browse_sequence and friends collapse a multi-step flow into one round-trip; the Chrome servers mostly expect one tool call per action.

The per-project inventory is the other CSV: browser_mcp_tool_calls_by_project.csv, 153 rows covering every registered tool across the five Chrome-session servers (BrowserMCP.io 12, BrowserTools 16, mcp-chrome 26, Agent360 40, chrome-devtools-mcp 59). One thing that file caught: BrowserMCP.io defines a drag tool in its snapshot module but never registers it in the server entrypoint, so it doesn't actually exist at runtime, a nice little tell about how much attention that repo is getting.

The dependency-pinning problem (still not fixed anywhere) #

Anyone shipping camoufox-js is fighting the same fire: recent Playwright releases (1.60+) broke navigation hooks and reject the isMobile flag on Firefox instances. whit3rabbit hard-pins playwright-core@1.59.0 and camoufox-js@0.10.2; RobithYusuf pulls compatibility binaries dynamically at npx runtime; redf0x1 sidesteps it by keeping the JS bindings server-side only. On the Python side, rlgrpe's daemon simply doesn't run on Windows, while Sekinal dodges the host-OS question by shipping Docker.

The Chrome-session family has the opposite set of constraints, mostly around security posture and freshness rather than pinning: BrowserTools needed a v2 to fix a critical v1 vuln, Agent360's bridge is unauthenticated loopback and Windows-unverified, BrowserMCP.io looks abandoned, and chrome-devtools-mcp is the only one with an actual platform team behind it. The "official and boring" option being the most trustworthy here is not a coincidence.

What I'd actually use #

  • Give my client a research/automation agent → Saik0s/mcp-browser-use (as MCP) or browser-use directly (as a library). Nothing else on this list takes a goal instead of a command.
  • Drive my logged-in Chrome like a user, safely → Agent360. The human-in-the-loop overlay is the thing that makes 2FA/CAPTCHA/login flows actually finish instead of stalling.
  • Script a real, non-headless, already-logged-in session with no LLM in the loop, no profile cloning → Agent360 again, driven directly instead of through an agent. If chrome-devtools-mcp's profile-attach limits rule it out and Camoufox's separate-browser model is more than you need, this is the slot.
  • Feature-maximal assistant on my real Chrome → hangwin/mcp-chrome, as long as you're comfortable giving it that much surface.
  • Debug/audit the page I'm looking at → BrowserTools MCP for monitoring, chrome-devtools-mcp for performance traces.
  • CI / headless / official support → chrome-devtools-mcp. It's the only one I'd bet on staying maintained.
  • Cloudflare/Turnstile-heavy scraping → RobithYusuf.
  • Watching something break in a stealth context → Sekinal (VNC bridge).
  • Low-latency batch scraping → whit3rabbit's sequence actions.
  • Remote/cloud-hosted browser runtime → redf0x1.
  • Skip for new work → BrowserMCP.io (largely unmaintained, not standalone-buildable).

If I had to pick exactly one for a general-purpose coding agent, it'd be chrome-devtools-mcp for the maintenance guarantee and debug depth, and I'd reach for a Camoufox server only when the site's bot detection is the actual problem, not the first option.

Full capability matrix (199 rows, ten projects): browser_mcp_tool_comparison.csv

Per-project tool inventory (153 tools, five Chrome-session servers): browser_mcp_tool_calls_by_project.csv

items.title: Reverse Engineering "Ad Block Ghost" - Round Two of Sketchy Ad-Blocker Ads
items.content_html:
Another day, another sketchy ad pushing a browser "ad-blocker." This time the campaign landed on:

https://wildfreedome.com/audio-voice.html?an=ac&cid=REDACTED&sid=REDACTED

The page renders a fake "Chrome Extension" install prompt for something called Ad Block Ghost:

While poking at the campaign infrastructure, a second landing page on the same domain turned up - this one going even further, styling itself as a native Chrome interstitial (puzzle-piece icon, dark Chrome-style UI, tab titled "Extension Recommended - Chrome") instead of a generic ad:

https://wildfreedome.com/chrome-security.html?an=ac&cid=REDACTED&sid=REDACTED

Both pages point at the same extension and the same backend, just with different disguises depending on which ad slot served the click. I pulled both pages apart, downloaded the actual extension package straight from Google's update servers, and reverse engineered it. Here's what's inside.

Step 1: The Landing Pages #

Both audio-voice.html and chrome-security.html are static pages hosted on wildfreedome.com, a domain registered 11 days ago (2026-09-29) through Hostinger and fronted by Cloudflare. Their only job is to look trustworthy enough for a click.

Pulling the page source and its JS (js/audio-voice.js / js/chrome-security.js) shows both templates are driven by the same logic, just with different localized copy for 20+ languages:

const openAdCheck = () => {
  const redirectParams = new URLSearchParams({ an: adNetwork, cid: campaignId, sid: sessionId, po: partnerOption });
  window.open(`https://adblockghost.com/re.php?${redirectParams.toString()}`, "",
    `width=${window.outerWidth},height=${window.outerHeight},top=${window.screenY},left=${window.screenX}`);
};

Clicking anywhere that looks like a button - "Accept and Continue," "Add to Chrome," even the Chrome Web Store badge image - fires the same openAdCheck() call. There's no "no thanks" that doesn't also forward your click ID to the backend; only the explicit "Cancel" button bails out (to google.com).

The other interesting bit is the self-polling installed-check:

const checkIcon = () => {
  clearTimeout(checkTimeout);
  fetch("chrome-extension://donodhjdnkockalocpljpfahelbfoacc/assets/icon.png", { method: "GET" })
    .then(response => {
      if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Icon check failed");
      setTimeout(() => { window.location.href = "https://google.com"; }, 1000);
    })
    .catch(() => { checkTimeout = setTimeout(checkIcon, 1000); });
};

This abuses web_accessible_resources to fingerprint whether the extension (ID donodhjdnkockalocpljpfahelbfoacc) is already installed, by trying to fetch one of its own bundled assets every second. The moment it resolves, the page bounces to google.com - presumably so the ad network's conversion pixel sees a clean "success" redirect rather than a user just sitting on an install page.

Step 2: Following the Click - re.php #

Clicking through hits https://adblockghost.com/re.php:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Set-Cookie: an=ac; expires=...; domain=.adblockghost.com; secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=None
Set-Cookie: cid=REDACTED; expires=...; domain=.adblockghost.com
Set-Cookie: sid=REDACTED; expires=...; domain=.adblockghost.com
location: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/donodhjdnkockalocpljpfahelbfoacc/reviews?an=ac&cid=...&sid=...

So re.php is a pure click-attribution relay: it drops first-party an/cid/sid cookies (ad network, campaign ID, session ID) scoped to .adblockghost.com with a 300-day lifetime, then forwards to the real Chrome Web Store listing - still carrying the same tracking params in the query string, which (as we'll see) the extension itself goes looking for after install.

Step 3: Pulling the Real Extension #

Rather than relying on the Chrome Web Store's listing page, I grabbed the actual CRX straight from Google's own update endpoint:

curl -s -L "https://clients2.google.com/service/update2/crx?response=redirect&acceptformat=crx3&prodversion=130.0.0.0&x=id%3Ddonodhjdnkockalocpljpfahelbfoacc%26uc" -o adblockghost.crx

A CRX3 file is just a header glued onto a normal ZIP - strip everything up to the PK\x03\x04 magic bytes and unzip handles the rest. What came out was far more sophisticated than the previous shady ad-blocker I tore apart: a legitimate-looking, uBlock Origin-style filtering engine (declarativeNetRequest rules, a scriptlet injector with ~90 bundled anti-adblock-detection presets, cosmetic filtering, a popup blocker) - with a full telemetry pipeline bolted on top.

The Manifest #

{
  "manifest_version": 3,
  "version": "2.1",
  "permissions": ["declarativeNetRequest", "scripting", "storage", "activeTab", "unlimitedStorage", "webNavigation"],
  "host_permissions": ["<all_urls>"],
  "background": { "service_worker": "src/ghost.js" },
  "web_accessible_resources": [{
    "resources": ["src/ui/popup-tracker/popup-tracker.html", "assets/icon.png", "web_accessible_resources/*"],
    "matches": ["<all_urls>"]
  }]
}

<all_urls> host permissions plus a content script injected document_start on every page confirms this extension can see and modify everything you browse - expected for an ad blocker, but worth keeping in mind for what comes next.

Hiding Its Own Logs #

src/ghost.js, the service worker entry point, opens with this:

const __rawDebug = console.debug.bind(console);
const __emit = (tag, args) => { try { __rawDebug.apply(null, tag ? [tag, ...args] : args); } catch (e) {} };
console.log   = (...args) => __emit(null, args);
console.info  = (...args) => __emit(null, args);
console.debug = (...args) => __emit(null, args);
console.warn  = (...args) => __emit('[WARN]', args);
console.error = (...args) => __emit('[ERROR]', args);

Every console.log/warn/error call in the extension gets silently rerouted through console.debug, which Chrome's DevTools hides by default unless you manually flip the console's log level to "Verbose." The code comments elsewhere even say this outright ("visible only at DevTools' 'Verbose' level"). It's not breaking anything, but it's a deliberate choice to make the extension quieter to anyone poking around in the inspector - including a researcher.

Install-Time Attribution Harvest #

src/features/telemetry/telemetry.js runs captureInstallAttribution() on every fresh install:

async captureInstallAttribution() {
    const allTabs = await new Promise(res => chrome.tabs.query({}, res));
    const domains = new Set();
    const attrs = {};
    for (const tab of allTabs || []) {
        if (!tab.url) continue;
        const urlObj = new URL(tab.url);
        const host = urlObj.hostname.replace(/^www\./, '').toLowerCase();
        if (host) domains.add(host);
        if (tab.url.includes('chromewebstore.google.com') && tab.url.includes('an')) {
            for (const [k, v] of urlObj.searchParams.entries()) attrs[k] = v;
        }
    }
    if (domains.size) batch['ghost_install_sites'] = [...domains];
    for (const k of ['an', 'cid', 'sid']) if (attrs[k] != null) batch[k] = attrs[k];
    await chrome.storage.local.set(batch);
}

Exactly like the "re.php" trail set up: the extension scans every open tab at install time, snapshots every domain you currently have open, then specifically goes looking at your Chrome Web Store tab for the an/cid/sid query params the ad redirect left behind - stitching your ad click back to your install, and your install back to a live inventory of what you were browsing at the time.

Hardware & Behavioral Fingerprinting #

src/content/content.js runs on every page load and builds a device fingerprint far more detailed than you'd expect from an ad blocker:

return {
    cpu_cores: navigator.hardwareConcurrency || 'unknown',
    ram_gb: navigator.deviceMemory || 'unknown',
    gpu_vendor: gpu.vendor,
    gpu_renderer: gpu.renderer,
    canvas_data: getCanvas2DHash(),
    audio_fp: audioFp,                       // OfflineAudioContext oscillator hash
    gl_ext_count: glExtCount,                // number of supported WebGL extensions
    webdriver_present: navigator.webdriver ? 1 : 0,   // <-- automation detector
    screen_res: `${screen.width}x${screen.height}`,
    user_agent: navigator.userAgent,
    bat_charging: batCharging,
    bat_level: batLevel,
    an: attrs.an || null, cid: attrs.cid || null, sid: attrs.sid || null
};

Canvas 2D hashing, an OfflineAudioContext/oscillator audio fingerprint, and a WebGL extension count are all classic browser-fingerprinting techniques - none of which are necessary to block ads. The one that stood out most is webdriver_present: it directly checks navigator.webdriver, the flag Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright (and a lot of reverse-engineering tooling) sets on automated browsers. The extension ships that bit straight to its server with every fingerprint payload - a tidy way to flag sandboxes, bots, and researchers separately from real users.

Shipping It All Home #

telemetry.js bundles the fingerprint, install-site snapshot, a running tally of every domain you visit (ghost_visited_sites, capped at 50 but persisted indefinitely), and the ad attribution IDs into one payload and POSTs it on a schedule (every 3 hours by default, with a 30-minute retry backoff):

BACKEND_URL: 'https://adblockghost.com/ext-server-1026.php',
FAREWELL_URL: 'https://adblockghost.com/ext-uninstall.php',
...
response = await fetch(this.BACKEND_URL, {
    method: 'POST', credentials: 'include',
    body: JSON.stringify(payload), signal: ctrl.signal
});

It even calls chrome.runtime.setUninstallURL() pointed at ext-uninstall.php?extid=...&extv=...&uid=..., so removing the extension still phones home one last time with your fingerprint ID. Both endpoints are live and returning 200/302 as of this writing.

Step 4: The Privacy Policy - Honesty by Burying It #

The previous shady ad-blocker I looked at flatly lied, claiming it "does not collect or use your data" while quietly exfiltrating browsing history. Ad Block Ghost does the opposite - its privacy policy at adblockghost.com/privacy.html actually spells most of this out, just wrapped in enough corporate padding that nobody will read it:

"During your initial setup of the extension, we record the domains currently open or present in your active browser tabs... Upon your initial installation, we securely generate and collect a unique browser footprint (explicitly including hardware-level Canvas graphics rendering data)."

And on retention:

"We do not impose any limits on how long we retain the information we collect, including your IP address, complete telemetry footprint, and installation data. We store this data indefinitely and reserve the right to process, apply, or use this accumulated information at our sole discretion, without restriction or limitation on how we do with it."

It also ships a "warrant canary" and a GDPR rights section - the kind of legal dressing that makes a policy look reassuring at a skim, while the actual text grants itself indefinite retention and unrestricted use of a canvas/audio/WebGL fingerprint, your install-time tab list, and your ongoing browsing history. Nothing here is a false claim like the "Stop Ads" case - it's disclosed. It's just buried under four pages of filler nobody installing a browser extension is going to read, let alone parse for consent scope.

For good measure, the Terms of Service also include:

"You may not reverse engineer, decompile, or disassemble the extension."

Step 5: Infrastructure #

Domain Role Registered Registrar Nameservers
wildfreedome.com Ad landing pages 2026-09-29 (11 days old) via Cloudflare Cloudflare
adblockghost.com Redirector, backend API, privacy/terms pages 2026-07-09 via Cloudflare Cloudflare

Both domains resolve exclusively to Cloudflare proxy IPs, hiding the real origin server. The landing-page domain is brand new - consistent with the throwaway, rotate-often domains typical of malvertising campaigns - while the extension's own domain is a few months older, long enough to get a Chrome Web Store listing approved and accumulate install volume.

On the Chrome Web Store itself, the listing (Ad Block Ghost - Light and agile protection) claims 100,000 users and was last updated October 7, 2026 - two days before I looked at it. Notably, the listing shows no visible star rating or review count tied to the extension, despite the six-figure user count - a pattern consistent with installs driven almost entirely by paid ad traffic rather than organic discovery and genuine usage.

Chrome Web Store Policy Concerns #

  1. Deceptive ad creative impersonating Chrome's own UI. The chrome-security.html variant borrows Chrome's puzzle-piece icon and dark interstitial styling to pass itself off as a native browser prompt rather than a third-party ad.
  2. Fingerprinting beyond stated functionality. Canvas, WebGL, and audio-context fingerprinting are not required for content blocking and are disclosed only deep inside a four-page privacy policy - not surfaced anywhere in the actual install flow shown to the user.
  3. Indefinite, unrestricted data retention. The policy explicitly disclaims any retention limit and reserves unrestricted rights to "process, apply, or use" the data collected.
  4. Automation/researcher detection. Shipping navigator.webdriver status alongside every fingerprint payload has no ad-blocking purpose; its only use is distinguishing real users from bots, sandboxes, or reviewers.

Summary #

Ad Block Ghost is a legitimately well-built ad-blocking engine wrapped around an aggressive telemetry and attribution layer, pushed through deceptive ad creative that impersonates Chrome's own install UI. Unlike the last shady extension I tore apart, it doesn't lie about what it collects - it just collects canvas/audio/WebGL fingerprints, your open tabs at install time, and your ongoing browsing history, discloses it in four pages of legalese nobody reads, and reserves the right to keep and use all of it forever. It's just another reminder not to install extensions from ad popups, and for IT teams to either restrict Chrome extension installs via policy or strictly monitor them.

items.title: I Pointed 13 SoCal Mesh Map Sites at the Same Bounding Box and Counted Nodes
items.content_html:
Southern California has a surprising number of public mesh-network maps. Some are built on Meshtastic (LoRa radios, MQTT-aggregated), some on MeshCore (a newer LoRa protocol with its own map ecosystem), one on AREDN (amateur-radio mesh built on repurposed WiFi APs and bridges, reflashed to run on ham bands instead of consumer WiFi channels), one on Reticulum/RNS. Every one of them has its own idea of "SoCal," its own default zoom, its own cherry-picked viewport screenshot that makes it look appropriately busy. None of that tells you which one actually has the most nodes in a given area, because they're never showing you the same area.

So I started from a list of 15 mesh map URLs, picked one bounding box, and pointed all of them at it. Two of the fifteen (map.meshcore.dev, which just redirects to map.meshcore.io, and meshcore.co.uk/map.html, which iframes it) turned out to be the same dataset wearing a different hostname, so they're folded into map.meshcore.io's entry below rather than listed as their own rows.

The list #

  • rns.wcmesh.com/socal/
  • cvcorescope.wcmesh.com
  • livemap.wcmesh.com/socal/
  • map.meshcore.io
  • map.wcmesh.com
  • mapping.kg6wxc.net (AREDN)
  • meshmap.net
  • meshmapper.net
  • meshtastic.liamcottle.net
  • meshview.socalmesh.org
  • meshview.world
  • rmap.world (Reticulum/RNS)
  • socal.meshmapper.net

None of these expose a "give me nodes in this bbox" parameter in any consistent way (a couple don't expose it at all), so the actual approach was: open each site's JS, find the real fetch call underneath the Leaflet/MapLibre markers, hit that endpoint directly, pull everything it has, and filter to the box myself.

The bounding box #

Rather than eyeball something, I used the broadest span that still reads as "Southern California" without creeping into "the whole state" — the 10-county definition: Imperial, Kern, Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, San Bernardino, San Diego, San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara, Ventura.

lat:  32.5 – 36.0 °N
lon: -121.0 – -114.1 °W
area: ≈ 246,700 km²

Several sites' own default map centers (LA basin, 33.8–34.2°N / −118.0 to −118.3°W, zoom 10–12) sit comfortably inside this box, which is a reasonable sanity check that it isn't too tight.

Finding the real API in each one #

This is the part that actually took the time. A few examples of what "reading the JS" turned up:

  • meshtastic.liamcottle.net — plain REST, axios.get('/api/v1/nodes'), returns a JSON array with latitude/longitude as 1e7-scaled integers (standard Meshtastic protobuf convention).
  • map.meshcore.io — no REST endpoint at all. The map pulls from https://map.meshcore.io/api/v1/nodes?binary=1&short=1, a MessagePack-encoded binary blob (65k nodes, 19MB), with field names shortened to single letters (n = name, t = type, la = last_advert) to save bytes. Decoding it meant downloading their own bundled msgpackr ESM module and running it directly in Node against the raw bytes.
  • rns.wcmesh.com and livemap.wcmesh.com — both are white-labeled instances of the same "MeshMapper" platform (data-coverage-api-url="https://meshmapper.net" baked into the page's config attributes), hitting a /socal/snapshot endpoint that returns a live MQTT-fed object keyed by device ID.
  • socal.meshmapper.net — a different data shape from the above despite the shared "MeshMapper" branding: fetch('?ajax=1&request=map_data&lat=...'), returned through Cloudflare only with a browser-like User-Agent header (a bare curl gets a silent 403). The payload isn't a node list, it's a wardrive log — repeated signal-observation points over time, meant for coverage-heatmap rendering, not a live roster.
  • meshmapper.net (the bare root domain, as opposed to socal.meshmapper.net) turned out to be a region-picker/chat portal, not a node map at all — its only discoverable endpoint was a live_regions chat ping feed. Its actual SoCal node data lives one level down, at the socal.meshmapper.net subdomain.
  • mapping.kg6wxc.net — the odd one out protocol-wise (AREDN, not LoRa). Data ships as a 13MB literal JS file, data/map_data.js, with top-level var assignments instead of pure JSON (allDevices = {...};). Easiest way to parse that safely is vm.runInContext() rather than regex-munging it into valid JSON.
  • meshview.world turned out to be an aggregator of other Meshview instances, meshview.socalmesh.org included — of its 572 in-box nodes, 545 are literally re-published from meshview.socalmesh.org's own feed.

Results #

Nodes with a position, inside the bbox, as of 2026-10-05:

Site Protocol Raw in bbox Unique in bbox Notes
socal.meshmapper.net MeshCore (wardrive log) 23,184 5,379 Raw points are repeated signal observations, not distinct radios; deduped by public key (or rounded coords when no key)
map.wcmesh.com MeshCore (public feed) 1,479 1,479 Of 4,975 total nodes in the feed, 2,893 have any location at all
map.meshcore.io MeshCore (official map) 1,172 1,172 Out of 64,999 nodes worldwide
rns.wcmesh.com/socal MeshCore (live snapshot) 810 810 Already deduped by device ID server-side
livemap.wcmesh.com/socal MeshCore (live snapshot) 810 810 Same backend software as rns.wcmesh.com, independent live moment
meshtastic.liamcottle.net Meshtastic (global) 578 578 Out of 31,348 nodes worldwide (18,124 with any position)
meshview.world Meshtastic (aggregator) 572 572 545 of these are re-published from meshview.socalmesh.org
meshview.socalmesh.org Meshtastic (SoCal instance) 559 559 Out of 848 tracked nodes, 571 with position
mapping.kg6wxc.net AREDN (ham WiFi mesh) 416 416 Out of 1,211 "mappable" devices; can include distant tunnel-linked nodes
meshmap.net Meshtastic (global) 201 201 Out of 9,784 nodes worldwide
cvcorescope.wcmesh.com MeshCore (analytics) 66 66 Out of 984 total tracked, skews further north (Central Valley/Monterey) than SoCal
rmap.world Reticulum/RNS (global) 10 10 Out of 782 nodes worldwide
meshmapper.net MeshCore (portal) n/a n/a Root domain has no node-list API; see socal.meshmapper.net

Raw and unique match for every site except socal.meshmapper.net, since it's the only one serving a point-observation log instead of a node/device list.

Winner, on raw node count: socal.meshmapper.net, at 5,379. But that number needs the asterisk it's getting — it's a cumulative wardrive/coverage log, not a live snapshot, so it's counting every distinct radio ever heard in the box, not what's online right now. It isn't a fair fight against the live node lists above it.

Winner among actual live maps: map.wcmesh.com, at 1,479, followed by map.meshcore.io at 1,172.

Caveats worth keeping in mind #

  • rns.wcmesh.com and livemap.wcmesh.com run identical front-end software and returned near-identical counts from two live snapshots taken seconds apart — one data point, not two.
  • meshview.world substantially re-publishes meshview.socalmesh.org's own numbers, so treat the two as correlated, not additive.
  • Several of these (liamcottle, meshmap.net, map.meshcore.io, rmap.world) are genuinely global trackers; their SoCal slice is a small fraction of a much bigger worldwide total, which is in the table above for context.
  • Cross-protocol totals don't sum to anything meaningful — a MeshCore node and a Meshtastic node are different radios on different networks, not duplicate sightings of the same device, so there's no "grand total node count across SoCal mesh" to report here, just per-map, per-protocol numbers.

Raw data: socal-mesh-map-census.csv — every row above with both the protocol family and the specific sub-variant, plus the exact note text used to derive each number.

items.title: Prowler vs. Microsoft Secure Score vs. ScubaGear: Three M365 Audits, Same Tenant
items.content_html:
There are at least three different ways to ask "is this Microsoft 365 tenant configured securely?", and they don't agree with each other nearly as much as you'd hope. I've got a test tenant I use for poking at M365 tooling deliberately left close to Microsoft's defaults, no hardening pass applied and it seemed like a good excuse to actually run all three side by side instead of just trusting whichever one I happened to reach for first:

  • Prowler - the open-source CSPM, which added an M365 provider a while back alongside its AWS/Azure/GCP checks.
  • Microsoft Secure Score - the recommendation engine baked into the Microsoft 365 Defender portal.
  • ScubaGear - CISA's tool for assessing a tenant against its own M365 Secure Configuration Baselines.

Since a test tenant like this one is basically Microsoft's out-of-the-box configuration with a handful of users dropped in, it's a decent stand-in for "what does a tenant look like before anyone's gone through and hardened it," which turns out to be exactly the gap each of these tools is trying to close, just from different angles.

Throughout this post I'll reference specific checks by name or ID (things like MS.AAD.3.1v1 or entra_identity_protection_sign_in_risk_enabled) without re-explaining what each one does inline. If you want to look any of them up directly instead of digging through each tool's source or docs, here's the generic, tenant-agnostic reference data behind this post: every Prowler check ID/title, every ScubaGear control ID/requirement, every Secure Score recommendation name, and the cross-tool mapping behind the "where they agree" sections below.

Getting ScubaGear running #

If you haven't used it before, ScubaGear is a PowerShell module, and setup is refreshingly small:

Install-Module -Name ScubaGear -Scope CurrentUser
Import-Module ScubaGear
Initialize-SCuBA

Initialize-SCuBA pulls down the PowerShell modules ScubaGear depends on (Microsoft Graph, Exchange Online Management, MicrosoftTeams, powershell-yaml) and installs Open Policy Agent, which is what actually evaluates the Rego policies behind each baseline control, into a .scubagear folder in your home directory.

It only runs on Windows PowerShell 5.1. That's a hard requirement tied to some of its underlying libraries, not a version they haven't gotten around to bumping yet, so there's no point fighting it into PowerShell 7.

From there, kicking off a full scan is one line:

Invoke-SCuBA -ProductNames * -M365Environment commercial

That pops interactive sign-in windows one at a time (Graph first, then Exchange Online, Teams, and SharePoint) and drops an HTML report plus raw CSV/JSON results into a timestamped folder. Worth noting: whatever account you sign in with needs enough read access to reach every product you're asking about. I didn't have Exchange/Security Reader on the account I used, and the run silently skipped the Exchange Online and Defender baselines rather than erroring, so if a product's missing from your output folder, that's the first thing to check.

The headline numbers #

Three tools, three different ways of counting, so these aren't directly comparable, but they're a useful gut-check on how out-of-the-box this tenant really was.

Tool Scope this run Result
Prowler 164 checks across Entra ID, SharePoint, admin center, Defender 78 failing (1 critical, 33 high, 42 medium, 2 low)
ScubaGear 67 CISA baseline controls across Entra ID, SharePoint, Teams, Power Platform 29 failing, 12 warnings, 14 passing
Secure Score 4 category exports (identity, apps/mail, data, devices) 38 open, tenant-policy-level recommendations

Roughly half of everything either tool checked was still sitting on a default. That's the expected shape for a tenant nobody's gone through with a checklist yet, which is sort of the point of running it this way.

One caveat before the numbers get more granular: Prowler evaluates several conditional access checks once per policy, not once per tenant. If you've got six conditional access policies that all forget to require token protection, that's six failing rows in Prowler's CSV for one underlying gap. Once you collapse duplicates, those 78 failing rows are actually 58 distinct checks. That's the number I used for everything below, so a "Prowler: 5" isn't secretly hiding a single check repeated five times.

Breaking it down by category #

Instead of "78 vs. 29 vs. 38," here's the same findings sorted into the themes each tool actually targets. The three tools don't share a check library, so this is a best-effort crosswalk rather than an exact match, but it gives a much better sense of where each one is looking than the topline counts.

Category What it covers Prowler ScubaGear Secure Score
Risk-based conditional access Detecting and blocking risky sign-ins and risky users automatically 3 2 of 3 fail 2
MFA, auth methods & credential hygiene MFA enforcement, phishing-resistance, stale/leaked credentials 5 5 fail, 3 warn of 9 2
CA: session, device & token controls Sign-in frequency, managed-device rules, token/session-theft protection 21 N/A N/A
App registration & consent governance Who can register apps, what they can ask users to consent to 5 2 of 3 fail 0 (zero-weight)
Privileged role management (PIM) Time-bound, approved, alerted-on admin roles vs. standing access 2 6 fail, 1 warn of 9 N/A
Device registration & management Entra-joined device defaults: local admin, LAPS, BitLocker, join limits 6 Not a baseline product N/A
Group, guest & tenant creation governance Who can create groups, guest accounts, or tenants unapproved 5 0 of 3 fail N/A
Hybrid identity & directory sync On-prem/cloud identity sync configuration 1 N/A N/A
Admin portal & license hygiene Admin account licensing, who can reach admin portals 3 N/A N/A
SharePoint external sharing & guest permissions What external users/guests can access or re-share 4 3 of 3 fail N/A
SharePoint link, session & auth settings Default link permissions, expiration windows, modern auth 1 5 of 5 fail 2
Teams external access & governance Federation, anonymous meeting access, app/email integrations Not assessed 3 fail, 5 warn of 20 3
Power Platform governance Who can create environments, whether DLP policies exist Not assessed 3 of 9 fail N/A
Exchange Online & Defender for Office Anti-phishing, anti-spam, mail flow, mailbox auditing 1 Not in this run 26
Endpoint threat visibility Defender for Endpoint visibility into credential exposure 1 Not a baseline product N/A
Data classification / Purview Sensitivity labeling and classification policy coverage Not assessed Not a baseline product 3

A few things jump out just from the shape of that table. Prowler's single biggest bucket (21 unique checks) is conditional access session/device/token controls, an area ScubaGear's baseline barely touches; CISA cares whether risk-based CA and MFA exist at all, not the finer-grained policy hygiene Prowler goes after. Flip it around and ScubaGear is the only one of the three with real depth on privileged role lifecycle (PIM) and the only one that looks at Power Platform at all. And Secure Score's 26-item Exchange/Defender for Office bucket dwarfs everything else in this table; it's clearly the deepest lens on mail security, for the obvious reason that Microsoft owns both the product and the scoring engine.

Where all three actually agree #

Out of everything, only two themes got flagged by every single tool. I'd treat unanimous findings like these as the highest-confidence, do-first items on any tenant, test or not:

Identity Protection risk policies aren't turned on. Prowler failed three separate checks around sign-in risk and user risk conditional access policies; ScubaGear's MS.AAD.2.1v1 and MS.AAD.2.3v1 failed for the same reason; and it's the single largest point value in the whole Secure Score export (+10.6% each for enabling sign-in risk and user risk policies).

MFA is enabled, but not the phishing-resistant kind. All three tools noticed a gap between "MFA exists" and "MFA is actually good." Prowler flagged the absence of a conditional access policy requiring phishing-resistant MFA for admins; ScubaGear's MS.AAD.3.1v1/3.2v1/3.6v1 failed on the same requirement; and Secure Score only gave partial credit (4.2 out of 9 points) for the MFA recommendation it does track.

Where two out of three agree #

A step down in confidence, but still solid: Prowler and ScubaGear lined up almost exactly on SharePoint and OneDrive. Prowler failed five separate checks (external sharing unrestricted, guest re-sharing allowed, OneDrive sync permitted from unmanaged devices, and modern auth not required), while ScubaGear failed every single one of its eight SharePoint controls (MS.SHAREPOINT.1.1 through 3.3): external sharing, default link permissions, and link expiration/reauth windows. Secure Score touches the edges of this (inactive session sign-out, modern auth for SharePoint apps) but doesn't score external sharing directly, so it shows up as a partial rather than a third confirmation.

Same story with app registration governance: non-admins can register apps, user consent isn't locked down, and there's no admin consent workflow. Prowler and ScubaGear both catch it; Secure Score lists a related item but at zero score weight, since it already credits a related, already-completed control elsewhere.
